job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Maya Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thank you for your time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing a one-year master's in information systems at Lindholm University, and I rent a room in a student block ten minutes' walk from campus. A normal day is a nine o'clock seminar, a few hours on my dissertation about how hospitals pick software, and a list on my phone of what to do before bed. My dad is an accountant and my mum teaches primary school, and they've said they'll back me, so I have no debt.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you do with the list?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I tick things off, honestly, and I'm a little proud of it. My bachelor's in computer science was a pass, not great, and I had no internship, because I took a summer job at a garden centre to pay for a trip. I use a chatbot now and then to summarise papers, but I check the summaries against the originals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's reasonable, and I'd probably say I told you so to a friend who's been panicking about it. At the seminar my tutor would nod and say tools come and go. Online I wouldn't say much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the plan holds: finish in September, apply for business analyst or systems support jobs, and expect a normal graduate salary. I have six months saved and no debt, and Lindholm has a lot of employers, from the hospital to two insurers. I'd be fine, even with a pass degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write a list of forty target employers and apply to ten a month from June. I'd ask my dad's colleague, who runs finance systems at an insurer, for a coffee. I'd also finish a small portfolio piece for my dissertation about hospital software, which I can show in interviews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I like it when the future is a lot like the present.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the job search look like in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to the hospital trust's IT team, two insurers, a council and a couple of consultancies. I'd spend an hour a day on applications rather than a big bang. I'd tell myself that ten rejections in a row are normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who gives you advice about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad, mostly. He tells me to make friends in places where I'd like to work, because a name on a list gets read faster than a stranger's. He's usually right, and it annoys me.

say: That's reasonable, and I'd tell a panicking friend I **told you so**.
My tutor would say tools **come and go**.
think: The plan holds: finish in September and apply for **business analyst** jobs.
I have six months saved and **no debt**, so a pass degree won't sink me.
do: Write a list of **forty employers** and apply to ten a month from June.
Meet my dad's colleague at an **insurer** for coffee and finish a portfolio piece.
feel: **Calm**: I like it when the future looks like the present.
S0.quote: I'd tell myself that ten rejections in a row are normal.
fieldNote: Her calm comes from a **list and a routine**, not from certainty about the market.
Mentions her pass degree and no internship but treats them as **fixable gaps**.

steps.text: Apply to ten employers a month from June
Meet my dad's colleague at an insurer for coffee
Finish the hospital software portfolio piece for interviews

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and people should be told clearly which tasks go. At the seminar I'd ask my tutor what the hospital's IT team would do differently. Online I'd share a sensible article, if I could find one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it hits exactly where I'm aiming. Business analysis, testing, documentation and support desks are the first places the tools reach. Employers might hire one graduate where they used to hire four, and I'd be one of four hundred. I have money, but my cushion isn't a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move my applications from generic analyst roles to jobs that need people: hospital IT with clinicians, client-facing roles at insurers, and project coordination. I'd learn two automation tools properly and add them to my CV. I'd also ask my university's careers office for a mock interview with an employer who actually hires.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm saving and I have a plan, but my stomach tightens when I read about hiring freezes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which entry jobs are you aiming at, and how exposed are they?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Roles with a person on the other side of the desk, like helping nurses with a new system. Tools can write the manual, but someone still has to sit with a nurse called Gill from ward six who hates the new screen. That's a job I can do and enjoy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your list change to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend less on going out, say eighty pounds a month less, and hold on to my reserve. I wouldn't spend savings on a second degree until I knew what pays. I'd rather do short, cheap courses and see.

say: It's a big change, and people should be told clearly **which tasks go**.
I'd ask my tutor what hospital IT would do **differently**.
think: It hits where I'm aiming: analysis, testing and **support desks**.
Employers might hire one graduate where they hired four, and my **cushion isn't a job**.
do: Shift applications to **people-facing** roles in hospital IT and insurers.
Learn two **automation tools** properly and add them to my CV.
feel: Anxious: I have a plan, but I tighten up at **hiring freeze** news.
S1.quote: Tools can write the manual, but someone still has to sit with a nurse called Gill from ward six who hates the new screen.
fieldNote: She reads the scenario as hitting her **exact target jobs** and re-aims toward people-facing work.
Won't spend on a **second degree** before knowing what pays, which is careful and practical.

steps.text: Aim applications at hospital IT roles that work with nurses
Learn two workflow automation tools and add them to my CV
Cut eighty pounds a month from going-out money
Keep the savings reserve and skip a second degree

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is serious and governments need a plan within the year. At the seminar I'd ask what the university will do for graduates. Online I'd stay measured, since I'm not an expert and don't want to add to panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd think the jobs I'm aiming for could be gone by the time I finish, or soon after. Full AGI by 2028 means any thinking work, including business analysis. The robots come around 2031, so physical jobs have a few more years, but I'm not a physical-jobs person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my parents the same week and show them my numbers: six months of savings and what I'd need per month. I'd finish the dissertation, since it's nearly done, and apply for jobs in places that must keep a human by law, like hospitals and courts. I'd also ask if my mum's school knows of any adult education roles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I make lists, but this time the list has too many question marks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, I have the savings to last about eight months, and I'll be careful. Dad would go over my budget with me, and Mum would say do what's sensible. I'd probably cry a bit in the car afterwards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does a master's even make sense in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably yes, to finish it, because dropping out now throws away what's been paid. I wouldn't start another degree, though. I'd put the energy into getting any job that gives me income and experience, even if it isn't my first choice.

say: This is serious, and governments need a **plan within the year**.
I'm not an expert, so I'd stay **measured** online.
think: The jobs I'm aiming for could be gone by the time I **finish**.
Physical jobs have a few more years, but I'm **not** a physical-jobs person.
do: Show my parents my **numbers**: six months saved and monthly needs.
Apply in places where the law keeps a **human**, like hospitals and courts.
feel: Anxious: the list I make has **too many question marks**.
S2.quote: I make lists, but this time the list has too many question marks.
fieldNote: Her **list habit** fails her here, which is how the fear shows up.
Turns to the **family budget** early and in the open, which is a sound response.

steps.text: Show my parents my savings and monthly budget
Finish the dissertation before taking any new course
Apply for hospital and court roles that must keep a human
Take any paid job that builds experience while I wait

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but it's enough to see what comes, so people should start preparing now. At the seminar I'd suggest the course adds a practical module. Online I'd say nothing, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd think I get a first job and maybe two years in it before the thinking AI takes over. The jobs I'm aiming for will thin out before then, so I'd end up in something more hands-on or people-heavy. It's less frightening than two years, but still not cosy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first reasonable job, probably hospital IT or an insurer, and save half my salary. I'd use the years to learn the actual workflows and the people, since those are hard to automate. By year three I'd retrain in something like medical device support if my job looked shaky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can work with. It feels like a long hill, not a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is the picture different with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask them for a bit of help with a deposit on a flat later, but only if it's needed. Mostly I'd ask for advice. Mum has seen what changes in schools, and she says the people who last are the ones who learn the names of the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with your parents' help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is a cliff and five is a long hill. With five I can learn how a hospital runs, who makes the decisions, and what they'd miss if a machine did my job. That knowledge is what I'd take with me.

say: Five years is short but enough to see what comes, so **start preparing now**.
I'd suggest the course adds a **practical module**.
think: I'd get a first job and about **two years** before thinking AI takes over.
The jobs I'm aiming for thin out first, so I'd end up in something **people-heavy**.
do: Take a hospital IT or **insurer** job and save half my salary.
Retrain in something like **medical device support** by year three if needed.
feel: Anxious, but workable: a long **hill**, not a cliff.
S3.quote: Two years is a cliff and five is a long hill.
fieldNote: Her **metaphor** captures how time changes the stress, from cliff to hill.
Plans to hold **workplace knowledge**, such as who decides what in a hospital, as her real asset, which software lacks.

steps.text: Take a hospital IT or insurer graduate job
Save half of every month's pay
Learn the hospital's workflows and who decides what
Retrain in medical device support if the job looks shaky

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives everyone a fair chance, and the colleges should add the right modules now. I'd tell friends to keep a list of skills they like and see what survives. Online I'd probably share the odd link.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be uneasy but fine. By 2036 I'd be thirty-four, with a decade in hospital IT, a family maybe, and a role that involves people as much as software. Robots come around 2039, and I'd be well past entry level.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start at a hospital or insurer, move up in a few years and take a part-time course in health informatics. I'd save steadily for a flat deposit and a family, and I'd learn the AI tools as they appear, since I use them now and then anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, like a rain forecast for next month. I'd carry an umbrella and still go out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with ten years that you can't with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the health informatics course, which takes two years part time, and switch to a role where I'm helping clinicians choose and test tools. With ten years I can be the person in the room who knows both sides. In two years I can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents would be in their sixties, so their pensions matter more than any job. Dad says pensions are mostly invested in shares, and he'd watch them. I'd tell them to keep it simple and not make big moves because of headlines.

say: Ten years gives everyone a **fair chance**, and colleges should add modules now.
I'd tell friends to keep a list of skills and see **what survives**.
think: By 2036 I'd have a decade in **hospital IT** and a role that involves people.
I'd be **uneasy** but fine, because I'm well past entry level.
do: Start at a hospital or insurer and take a part-time **health informatics** course.
Save steadily for a **flat deposit** and learn AI tools as they arrive.
feel: Uneasy, like a **rain forecast** for next month: I'd carry an umbrella and go out.
S4.quote: I'd carry an umbrella and still go out.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her plan a **career ladder** and a family together.
Worries about her **parents' pensions** more than any job, which widens her view beyond herself.

steps.text: Start at a hospital or insurer and aim for a promotion in three years
Study health informatics part time over two years
Save steadily for a flat deposit
Tell my parents not to move pensions on headlines

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most. My list of jobs would be pointless and my parents would be worried about me and their own pensions at the same time. What would help is a clear government plan, early warning from employers, and short, cheap courses that lead to real jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm not a panicker. I plan, but this subject is the first one where my planning feels thin.

headlineQuote: I plan, but this subject is the first one where my planning feels thin.
portrait: Maya is a **24-year-old** information systems master's student with a pass degree, six months saved and no debt.
She is a list-maker who uses AI **now and then** and checks its summaries against the originals.
She is centre and steady: she takes **cautious** steps, but only after the evidence arrives.
Her mood is calm in the mild world and **anxious** wherever desk-based entry jobs are at risk.
Her best bet is **people-facing** work in hospitals, where she knows the workflows and the staff.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, since her target jobs and her parents' pensions would be at risk together.
whatWouldHelp: A clear government **plan**, early warning from employers and cheap courses that lead to real jobs.
